=Φ−t​(λ⁡(ξ)​p​(z)).\displaystyle=\Phi_{-t}(\lambda(\xi)p(z)).

Replacing tt be −t-t in the equation above, we get Eq. (2.20).  □\Box

Proposition 2.6.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, the following statements hold.

(a)(a) The subspaces ℂ⁡[ξ]\mathbb{C}[\xi] and ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] are closed under the product ∗t\ast_{t} and hence, are actually subalgebras of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

(b)(b) As associative algebras, (ℂ[ξ],∗t)(\mathbb{C}[\xi],\ast_{t}) and (ℂ[z],∗t)(\mathbb{C}[z],\ast_{t}) are identical as the usual polynomial algebras 𝒜⁡[ξ]{\mathcal{A}}[\xi] and 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] in ξ\xi and zz, respectively.

(c)(c) ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] is a commutative free algebra generated freely by ξi\xi_{i} and ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). The set of the monomials generated by ξi\xi_{i} and ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) in ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] is given by {ξα∗tzβ|α,β∈ℕn}\{\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta}\,|\,\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\}.

Proof:  Note that (a)(a) and (b)(b) follow immediately from Eqs. (2.11) and (2.12).

To show (c)(c), first, by Eqs. (2.18) and (2.19), we know that the algebra isomorphism Φ−t=Φt−1:𝒜⁡[ξ,z]→ℬt​[ξ,z]\Phi_{-t}=\Phi_{t}^{-1}:{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] as a linear map from ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] to ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] fixes ξi\xi_{i} and ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). Hence, ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] is a commutative free algebra generated freely by ξi\xi_{i} and ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).

The second part of (c)(c) follows from Eqs. (2.11), (2.12) and the fact that the product ∗t\ast_{t} is associative and commutative.  □\Box

The next two lemmas will be needed in Subsection 5.3.

Lemma 2.7.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} and α,β∈ℕ\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}},

(2.21) (z∂−ξδ)(ξα∗tzβ)=(|β|−|α|)(ξα∗tzβ),\displaystyle(z\partial-\xi\delta)(\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta})=(|\beta|-|\alpha|)(\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta}),

where z∂−ξδ:=∑i=1n(zi∂i−ξiδi)z\partial-\xi\delta\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(z_{i}\partial_{i}-\xi_{i}\delta_{i}).

Proof:  First, by Euler’s lemma, we have

(2.22) (z∂−ξδ)(ξαzβ)=(|β|−|α|)(ξαzβ).\displaystyle(z\partial-\xi\delta)(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta})=(|\beta|-|\alpha|)(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta}).

Second, note that z∂−ξδz\partial-\xi\delta commutes with Λ\Lambda, hence also with Φt\Phi_{t} for any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}. Apply Φ−t\Phi_{-t} to Eq. (2.22), we get

(z∂−ξδ)Φ−t(ξαzβ)=(|β|−|α|)Φ−t(ξαzβ).\displaystyle(z\partial-\xi\delta)\Phi_{-t}(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta})=(|\beta|-|\alpha|)\Phi_{-t}(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta}).

Then, by Eq. (2.20) with tt replaced by −t-t, Eq. (2.21) follows from the equation above.  □\Box

Lemma 2.8.

For any λi​(ξ)∈ℂ​[ξ]\lambda_{i}(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi] and pi​(z)∈ℂ​[z]p_{i}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] (i=1,2)(i=1,2), we have

(2.23) (λ1​(ξ)​p1​(z))∗t(λ2​(ξ)​p2​(z))=(λ1​(ξ)∗tp2​(z))​(λ2​(ξ)∗tp1​(z)).\displaystyle(\lambda_{1}(\xi)p_{1}(z))\ast_{t}(\lambda_{2}(\xi)p_{2}(z))=(\lambda_{1}(\xi)\ast_{t}p_{2}(z))\,(\lambda_{2}(\xi)\ast_{t}p_{1}(z)).

Proof:  First, by Eq. (2.7), we have

(λ1​(ξ)​p1​(z))∗t(λ2​(ξ)​p2​(z))\displaystyle\quad(\lambda_{1}(\xi)p_{1}(z))\ast_{t}(\lambda_{2}(\xi)p_{2}(z))
=∑α,β∈ℕn(−t)|α|+|β|α!​β!​((δα​λ1​(ξ))​(∂βp1​(z)))​((δβ​λ2​(ξ))​(∂αp2​(z)))\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{(-t)^{|\alpha|+|\beta|}}{\alpha!\beta!}\left((\delta^{\alpha}\lambda_{1}(\xi))(\partial^{\beta}p_{1}(z))\right)\left((\delta^{\beta}\lambda_{2}(\xi))(\partial^{\alpha}p_{2}(z))\right)
Taking sum over α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and applying Eq. (2.13):
=(λ1​(ξ)∗tp2​(z))​∑β∈ℕn(−t)|β|β!​(∂βp1​(z))​(δβ​λ2​(ξ))\displaystyle=(\lambda_{1}(\xi)\ast_{t}p_{2}(z))\sum_{\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{(-t)^{|\beta|}}{\beta!}(\partial^{\beta}p_{1}(z))(\delta^{\beta}\lambda_{2}(\xi))
Taking sum over β∈ℕn\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and applying Eq. (2.13):
=(λ1​(ξ)∗tp2​(z))​(λ2​(ξ)∗tp1​(z)).\displaystyle=(\lambda_{1}(\xi)\ast_{t}p_{2}(z))(\lambda_{2}(\xi)\ast_{t}p_{1}(z)).

Hence we get Eq. (2.23).  □\Box

2.2. The ℓ\ell-adic Topologies Induced by ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] on ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]

We have seen that the algebras ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}) share the same base vector space ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] and, by Proposition 2.6, (c)(c), they are all commutative free algebras generated freely by ξ\xi and zz. Therefore, we may talk about the ℓ\ell-adic topologies on ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] induced by the algebras ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}), which are defined as follows.

For any t∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]t\in\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] and m≥0m\geq 0, set Ut,mU_{t,m} to be the subspace of ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] spanned by the monomials ξα∗tzβ\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta} of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] with α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and |α+β|≥m|\alpha+\beta|\geq m. The ℓ\ell-adic topology induced from the algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] is the topology whose open subsets are the subsets generated by Ut,mU_{t,m} (m∈ℕ)(m\in{\mathbb{N}}) and their translations by elements of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]. We denote by 𝒯t{\mathcal{T}}_{t} this topology on ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z].

The main result of this subsection is the following proposition.

Proposition 2.9.

(a)(a) For any s≠t∈ℂs\neq t\in\mathbb{C}, we have 𝒯s≠𝒯t{\mathcal{T}}_{s}\neq{\mathcal{T}}_{t}.

(b)(b) For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, the algebra isomorphism Φt:(ℬt​[ξ,z],𝒯t)→(𝒜⁡[ξ,z],𝒯0)\Phi_{t}:({\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}],{\mathcal{T}}_{t})\to({\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}],{\mathcal{T}}_{0}) is also a homeomorphism of topological spaces. Consequently, (ℬt​[ξ,z],𝒯t)({\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}],{\mathcal{T}}_{t}) (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}) as topological spaces are all homeomorphic.

Proof:  (a)(a) Let {αm∈ℕn|m≥1}\{\alpha_{m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\,|\,m\geq 1\} be any sequence of elements of ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that |αm|=m|\alpha_{m}|=m for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Set um:=ξαm∗tzαmu_{m}\!:=\xi^{\alpha_{m}}\ast_{t}z^{\alpha_{m}} for any m≥1m\geq 1. Then, by the definition of 𝒯t{\mathcal{T}}_{t}, we see that the sequence {um}\{u_{m}\} converges to 0∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]0\in\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] with respect to the topology 𝒯t{\mathcal{T}}_{t}.

But, on the other hand, set r:=s−t≠0r:=s-t\neq 0. Then, by Eq. (2.14), we have

um\displaystyle u_{m} =ξαm∗tzαm=(ξ−t∂)αmzαm=((ξ−s∂)+r∂)αmzαm\displaystyle=\xi^{\alpha_{m}}\ast_{t}z^{\alpha_{m}}=(\xi-t\partial)^{\alpha_{m}}z^{\alpha_{m}}=((\xi-s\partial)+r\partial)^{\alpha_{m}}z^{\alpha_{m}}
=∑β,γ∈ℕnβ+γ=αm(αmγ)(ξ−s∂)γ(∂βzαm)\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta,\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\\ \beta+\gamma=\alpha_{m}\end{subarray}}\binom{\alpha_{m}}{\gamma}(\xi-s\partial)^{\gamma}(\partial^{\beta}z^{\alpha_{m}})
=∑β,γ∈ℕnβ+γ=αm(αmγ)​ξγ∗s(∂βzαm)≡αm!mod(Us,0).\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta,\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\\ \beta+\gamma=\alpha_{m}\end{subarray}}\binom{\alpha_{m}}{\gamma}\xi^{\gamma}\ast_{s}(\partial^{\beta}z^{\alpha_{m}})\equiv\alpha_{m}!\mod(U_{s,0}).

From the equation above, we see that the sequence {um}\{u_{m}\} does not converge to 0∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]0\in\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] with respect to the topology 𝒯s{\mathcal{T}}_{s}. Hence 𝒯s≠𝒯t{\mathcal{T}}_{s}\neq{\mathcal{T}}_{t}.

(b)(b) Note that ℬt=0​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t=0}[{\xi,z}] is the usual polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] and Φt:ℬt​[ξ,z]→𝒜⁡[ξ,z]\Phi_{t}:{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] is an algebra isomorphism. Furthermore, from Eqs. (2.1), (2.18) and (2.19), we have

(2.24) Φt​(ξα∗tzβ)=ξα​zβ\displaystyle\Phi_{t}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta})=\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta}

for any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Therefore, for any m≥0m\geq 0, we have, Φt​(Ut,m)=U0,m\Phi_{t}(U_{t,m})=U_{0,m} and Φt−1​(U0,m)=Ut,m\Phi_{t}^{-1}(U_{0,m})=U_{t,m}. Hence, we have (b)(b).  □\Box

Actually, the proof above also shows that Proposition 2.9 also holds for the following topologies on ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] induced by the free algebras ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}).

For any t∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]t\in\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] and m≥0m\geq 0, set

(2.25) Ut,m′:=∑α∈ℕn;|α|≥mξα∗tℂ⁡[z].\displaystyle U_{t,m}^{\prime}\!:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n};\,\\ |\alpha|\geq m\end{subarray}}\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}\mathbb{C}[z].

Denote by 𝒯t′{\mathcal{T}}^{\prime}_{t} the topology on ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] generated by Ut,m′U_{t,m}^{\prime} and their translations (as open subsets). Then, by a similar argument as in the proof of Proposition 2.9, it is easy to see that the following corollary also holds.

Corollary 2.10.

(a)(a) For any s≠t∈ℂs\neq t\in\mathbb{C}, we have 𝒯s′≠𝒯t′{\mathcal{T}}_{s}{}^{\prime}\neq{\mathcal{T}}_{t}{}^{\prime}.

(b)(b) For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, the algebra isomorphism Φt:(ℬt[ξ,z],𝒯t)′→(𝒜[ξ,z],𝒯0)′\Phi_{t}:({\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}],{\mathcal{T}}_{t}{}^{\prime})\to({\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}],{\mathcal{T}}_{0}{}^{\prime}) is also a homeomorphism of topological spaces.

Note that, due to the symmetric roles played by ξ\xi and zz, the corollary above also holds if ξ\xi in Eq. (2.25) is replaced by zz.

2.3. The Induced Isomorphism (Φt)∗(\Phi_{t})_{\ast} on Differential Operator Algebras

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, denote by 𝒟t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] the differential operator algebra or the Weyl algebra of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}], i.e. the associative algebra generated by the ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivations and the multiplication operators of the algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]. Since Φt:ℬt​[ξ,z]→𝒜⁡[ξ,z]\Phi_{t}:{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] is an algebra isomorphism (See Corollary 2.2), it induces an algebra isomorphism, denoted by (Φt)∗:𝒟t​[ξ,z]→𝒟⁡[ξ,z](\Phi_{t})_{*}:{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{D}}[{\xi,z}], from the Weyl algebra 𝒟t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] to the Weyl algebra 𝒟⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}[{\xi,z}] of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}].

Recall that the induced map (Φt)∗(\Phi_{t})_{*} is defined by setting

(2.26) (Φt)∗​(ψ)=Φt∘ψ∘Φt−1=Φt∘ψ∘Φ−t\displaystyle(\Phi_{t})_{*}(\psi)=\Phi_{t}\circ\psi\circ\Phi_{t}^{-1}=\Phi_{t}\circ\psi\circ\Phi_{-t}

for any ψ∈𝒟t​[ξ,z]\psi\in{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

The main result of this subsection are the following two propositions, even though their proofs are very simple.

Proposition 2.11.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, the following statements hold.

(a)(a) ∂i\partial_{i} and δi\delta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) are also derivations of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

(b)(b) For any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, we have

(2.27) (Φt)∗(∂i)\displaystyle(\Phi_{t})_{*}(\partial_{i}) =∂i,\displaystyle=\partial_{i},
(2.28) (Φt)∗​(δi)\displaystyle(\Phi_{t})_{*}(\delta_{i}) =δi,\displaystyle=\delta_{i},

Proof:  Note first that ∂i\partial_{i} and δi\delta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) commute with Λ\Lambda, hence also with Φt\Phi_{t} for any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}. Then, Eqs. (2.27) and (2.28) follows immediately from this fact and the definition of (Φt)∗(\Phi_{t})_{*} given in Eq. (2.26).

(a)(a) follows from the general fact that the induced map of any algebra isomorphism maps derivations to derivations. It can also be checked directly as follows.

For any f,g∈ℬt​[ξ,z]f,g\in{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}], by Eq. (2.1) and the fact that ∂i\partial_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) commute with Φt\Phi_{t} (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}), we have

∂i(f∗tg)\displaystyle\partial_{i}(f\ast_{t}g) =∂i(Φ−t​(Φt​(f)​Φt​(g)))=Φ−t​(∂i(Φt​(f)​Φt​(g)))\displaystyle=\partial_{i}\Big(\Phi_{-t}\big(\Phi_{t}(f)\Phi_{t}(g)\big)\Big)=\Phi_{-t}\Big(\partial_{i}\big(\Phi_{t}(f)\Phi_{t}(g)\big)\Big)
=Φ−t​((∂iΦt​(f))​Φt​(g))+Φ−t​(Φt​(f)​(∂iΦt​(g)))\displaystyle=\Phi_{-t}\big((\partial_{i}\Phi_{t}(f))\Phi_{t}(g)\big)+\Phi_{-t}\big(\Phi_{t}(f)(\partial_{i}\Phi_{t}(g))\big)
=Φ−t​(Φt​(∂if)​Φt​(g))+Φ−t​(Φt​(f)​Φt​(∂ig))\displaystyle=\Phi_{-t}\big(\Phi_{t}(\partial_{i}f)\Phi_{t}(g)\big)+\Phi_{-t}\big(\Phi_{t}(f)\Phi_{t}(\partial_{i}g)\big)
=(∂if)∗tg+f∗t(∂ig).\displaystyle=(\partial_{i}f)\ast_{t}g+f\ast_{t}(\partial_{i}g).

Similarly, we can show that δi\delta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) are also derivations of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].  □\Box

Corollary 2.12.

For any α,β,γ∈ℕn\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(2.29) ∂γ(ξα∗tzβ)\displaystyle\partial^{\gamma}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta}) =γ!​(βγ)​(ξα∗tzβ−γ),\displaystyle=\gamma!\,\binom{\beta}{\gamma}\,(\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta-\gamma}),
(2.30) δγ​(ξα∗tzβ)\displaystyle\delta^{\gamma}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta}) =γ!​(αγ)​(ξα−γ∗tzβ).\displaystyle=\gamma!\,\binom{\alpha}{\gamma}\,(\xi^{\alpha-\gamma}\ast_{t}z^{\beta}).

Proof:  Note that, by Eqs. (2.11) and (2.12), we know that, for any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, ξα∗tzβ\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}z^{\beta} will remain the same if we replace the (usual) product of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] in the factors ξα\xi^{\alpha} and zβz^{\beta} by the product ∗t\ast_{t} of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]. By Proposition 2.11, (a)(a), we know that ∂i\partial_{i} and δi\delta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) are also the derivations of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]. From these two facts, it is easy to see that both equations in the corollary hold.  □\Box

Proposition 2.13.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} and f⁡(ξ,z)∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]f(\xi,z)\in\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}], (Φt)∗(\Phi_{t})_{*} maps the multiplication operator of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] by f⁡(ξ,z)f(\xi,z) ((with respect to the product ∗t\ast_{t})) to the multiplication operator of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] by Φt​(f​(ξ,z))\Phi_{t}(f(\xi,z)) ((with respect to the product of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}])).

Proof:  We denote by ψf\psi_{f} the multiplication operator of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] by f⁡(ξ,z)f(\xi,z) ((with respect to the product ∗t\ast_{t})). Then for any u⁡(ξ,z)∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]u({\xi,z})\in\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}], by Eqs. (2.26) and (2.1) we have

(Φt)∗​(ψf)​u​(ξ,z)\displaystyle(\Phi_{t})_{*}(\psi_{f})u({\xi,z}) =(Φt∘ψf∘Φt−1)​u​(ξ,z)=Φt​(f⁡(ξ,z)∗tΦt−1​(u⁡(ξ,z)))\displaystyle=(\Phi_{t}\circ\psi_{f}\circ\Phi_{t}^{-1})u({\xi,z})=\Phi_{t}\big(f(\xi,z)\ast_{t}\Phi_{t}^{-1}(u({\xi,z}))\big)
=Φt​(f⁡(ξ,z))​Φt​(Φt−1​(u⁡(ξ,z)))=Φt​(f⁡(ξ,z))​u​(ξ,z).\displaystyle=\Phi_{t}(f(\xi,z))\,\Phi_{t}\big(\Phi_{t}^{-1}(u(\xi,z))\big)=\Phi_{t}(f(\xi,z))\,u({\xi,z}).

Hence, the proposition follows.  □\Box

By the proposition above and Eqs. (2.18) and (2.19), we also have the following corollary.

Corollary 2.14.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, λ⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]\lambda(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi] and p⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]p(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], (Φt)∗(\Phi_{t})_{*} maps the multiplication operators of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] by λ⁡(ξ)\lambda(\xi) and p⁡(z)p(z) ((with respect to the product ∗t\ast_{t})) to the multiplication operators of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] by λ⁡(ξ)\lambda(\xi) and p⁡(z)p(z) ((with respect to the product of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}])), respectively.

Note that, as pointed out before, the algebras ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}) share the same base vectors space ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]. Therefore, their Weyl algebras 𝒟t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}) are all subalgebras of the algebra of linear endomorphisms of ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]. The following corollary says that all these subalgebras turn out to be same, i.e. they do not depend on the parameter t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}.

Corollary 2.15.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, as subalgebras of the algebra of linear endomorphisms of ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z], 𝒟t​[ξ,z]=𝒟⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]={\mathcal{D}}[{\xi,z}].

Proof:  By Proposition 2.6, (c)(c), we know that ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] is a commuative free algebra generated freely by ξ\xi and zz. By Proposition 2.11, (a)(a), we know that ∂i\partial_{i} and δi\delta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) are also derivations of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]. Therefore, the Weyl algebra 𝒟t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] as an associative algebra over ℂ\mathbb{C} is generated by the derivations ∂i\partial_{i}, δi\delta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) and the multiplication operators (with respect to the product ∗t\ast_{t}) by ξi,zi∈ℬt​[ξ,z]\xi_{i},z_{i}\in{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).

By Eqs. (2.14) and (2.15), we see that the multiplication operators by ξi,zi∈ℬt​[ξ,z]\xi_{i},z_{i}\in{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) are same as the operators ξi−t∂i\xi_{i}-t\partial_{i} and zi−t​δiz_{i}-t\delta_{i} which lie in 𝒟⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}[{\xi,z}]. Hence we have 𝒟t​[ξ,z]⊆𝒟⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]\subseteq{\mathcal{D}}[{\xi,z}].

To show 𝒟⁡[ξ,z]⊆𝒟t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}[{\xi,z}]\subseteq{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}], by Proposition 2.11, (a)(a), it will be enough to show that the multiplication operators (with respect to the product of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}]) by ξi,zi∈𝒜⁡[ξ,z]\xi_{i},z_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) also belong to 𝒟t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

But, for any f⁡(ξ,z)∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]f({\xi,z})\in\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}], by Eqs. (2.14) and (2.15), we have

ξi​f​(ξ,z)\displaystyle\xi_{i}f({\xi,z}) =(ξi−t∂i)f(ξ,z)+t∂if(ξ,z)=ξi∗tf(ξ,z)+t∂if(ξ,z),\displaystyle=(\xi_{i}-t\partial_{i})f({\xi,z})+t\partial_{i}f({\xi,z})=\xi_{i}\ast_{t}f({\xi,z})+t\partial_{i}f({\xi,z}),
zi​f​(ξ,z)\displaystyle z_{i}f({\xi,z}) =(zi−t​δi)​f​(ξ,z)+t​δi​f​(ξ,z)=zi∗tf⁡(ξ,z)+t​δi​f​(ξ,z).\displaystyle=(z_{i}-t\delta_{i})f({\xi,z})+t\delta_{i}f({\xi,z})=z_{i}\ast_{t}f({\xi,z})+t\delta_{i}f({\xi,z}).

From the equations above, we see that the multiplication operators (with respect to the product of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}]) by ξi,zi∈𝒜⁡[ξ,z]\xi_{i},z_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) do belong to 𝒟t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{D}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].  □\Box

3. Connections with Interchanges of Right and Left Total Symbols of Differential Operators

In this section, we show in Theorem 3.1 that the isomorphisms Φt\Phi_{t} with t=±1t=\pm 1 coincide with the interchanges between total left and right symbols of differential operators of the polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

First, let us fix the following notation and convention for the differential operators of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

We denote by 𝒟⁡[z]{\mathcal{D}}[z] the differential operator algebra or the Weyl algebra of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z]. For any differential operator ϕ∈𝒟⁡[z]\phi\in{\mathcal{D}}[z] and polynomial u⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z]u(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z], the notation ϕ​u​(z)\phi\,u(z) usually denotes the composition of ϕ\phi and the multiplication operator by u⁡(z)u(z). So ϕ​u​(z)\phi\,u(z) is still a differential operator of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z]. The polynomial obtained by applying ϕ\phi to u⁡(z)u(z) will be denoted by ϕ⁡(u⁡(z))\phi(u(z)).

Next, let us recall the right and left total symbols of differential operators of the polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

For any ϕ∈𝒟⁡[z]\phi\in{\mathcal{D}}[z], it is well-known (e.g. see Proposition 2.2 (pp. 4) in [B] or Theorem 3.1 (pp. 58) in [C]) that ϕ\phi can be written uniquely as the following two finite sums:

(3.1) ϕ=∑α∈ℕnaα(z)∂α=∑β∈ℕn∂βbβ(z)\displaystyle\phi=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}a_{\alpha}(z)\partial^{\alpha}=\sum_{\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\partial^{\beta}b_{\beta}(z)

where aα​(z),bβ​(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]a_{\alpha}(z),b_{\beta}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] but denote the multiplication operators by aα​(z)a_{\alpha}(z) and bβ​(z)b_{\beta}(z), respectively.

For the differential operator ϕ∈𝒟⁡[z]\phi\in{\mathcal{D}}[z] in Eq. (3.1), the right and left total symbols are defined to be the polynomials ∑α∈ℕnaα​(z)​ξα∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}a_{\alpha}(z)\xi^{\alpha}\in\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] and ∑β∈ℕnbβ​(z)​ξβ∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\sum_{\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}b_{\beta}(z)\xi^{\beta}\in\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}], respectively. We denote by ℛ:𝒟⁡[z]→ℂ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{R}}:{\mathcal{D}}[z]\to\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] (resp. ℒ:𝒟⁡[z]→ℂ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{L}}:{\mathcal{D}}[z]\to\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]) the linear map which maps any ϕ∈𝒟⁡[z]\phi\in{\mathcal{D}}[z] to its right total symbol (resp. left total symbol).

Note that, by the uniqueness of the expressions in Eq. (3.1), both ℛ{\mathcal{R}} and ℒ{\mathcal{L}} are isomorphisms of vector spaces over ℂ\mathbb{C}. The interchange of the left (resp. right) total symbol of differential operators to their right (resp. left) total symbols is given by the isomorphism ℛ∘ℒ−1{\mathcal{R}}\circ{\mathcal{L}}^{-1} (resp. ℒ∘ℛ−1{\mathcal{L}}\circ{\mathcal{R}}^{-1}) from ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] to ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z].

The main result of this section is the following theorem.

Theorem 3.1.

As linear maps from ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] to ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z], we have

(3.2) Φ\displaystyle\Phi =ℛ∘ℒ−1.\displaystyle={\mathcal{R}}\circ{\mathcal{L}}^{-1}.
(3.3) Φt=−1\displaystyle\Phi_{t=-1} =ℒ∘ℛ−1.\displaystyle={\mathcal{L}}\circ{\mathcal{R}}^{-1}.

Proof:  Note first that, Eq. (3.3) follows from Eq. (3.2) and the fact that Φt=−1=Φt=1−1=Φ−1\Phi_{t=-1}=\Phi_{t=1}^{-1}=\Phi^{-1}.

To show Eq. (3.2), since both Φ\Phi and ℛ∘ℒ−1{\mathcal{R}}\circ{\mathcal{L}}^{-1} are linear maps, it is enough to show that, for any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(3.4) Φ⁡(ξα​zβ)=(ℛ∘ℒ−1)​(ξα​zβ).\displaystyle\Phi(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta})=({\mathcal{R}}\circ{\mathcal{L}}^{-1})(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta}).

Since

(3.5) (ℛ∘ℒ−1)​(ξα​zβ)=ℛ⁡(∂αzβ),\displaystyle({\mathcal{R}}\circ{\mathcal{L}}^{-1})(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta})={\mathcal{R}}(\partial^{\alpha}z^{\beta}),

so we have to find the right total symbol of the differential operator ∂αzβ∈𝒟⁡[z]\partial^{\alpha}z^{\beta}\in{\mathcal{D}}[z].

Note that, for any dummy u⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]u(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], by the Leibniz rule, we have

(3.6) ∂α(zβ​u​(z))\displaystyle\partial^{\alpha}(z^{\beta}u(z)) =∑γ∈ℕn(αγ)⁡(∂γzβ)​(∂α−γu⁡(z))\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\binom{\alpha}{\gamma}(\partial^{\gamma}z^{\beta})(\partial^{\alpha-\gamma}u(z))
=(∑γ∈ℕn(αγ)(∂γzβ)∂α−γ)u(z).\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\binom{\alpha}{\gamma}(\partial^{\gamma}z^{\beta})\partial^{\alpha-\gamma}\right)u(z).

Therefore, the right total symbol of the differential operator ∂αzβ∈𝒟⁡[z]\partial^{\alpha}z^{\beta}\in{\mathcal{D}}[z] is given by

ℛ⁡(∂αzβ)\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}(\partial^{\alpha}z^{\beta}) =∑γ∈ℕn(αγ)⁡(∂γzβ)​ξα−γ=∑γ∈ℕn(αγ)​ξα−γ​(∂γzβ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\binom{\alpha}{\gamma}(\partial^{\gamma}z^{\beta})\xi^{\alpha-\gamma}=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\binom{\alpha}{\gamma}\xi^{\alpha-\gamma}(\partial^{\gamma}z^{\beta})
=∑γ∈ℕn1γ!​(δγ​ξα)​(∂γzβ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{1}{\gamma!}(\delta^{\gamma}\xi^{\alpha})(\partial^{\gamma}z^{\beta})

Combining the equation above with Eqs. (2.13) and (2.20) with t=−1t=-1, we have

(3.7) ℛ⁡(∂αzβ)=ξα∗t=−1zβ=Φt=1​(ξα​zβ)=Φ⁡(ξα​zβ).\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}(\partial^{\alpha}z^{\beta})=\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t=-1}z^{\beta}=\Phi_{t=1}(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta})=\Phi(\xi^{\alpha}z^{\beta}).

Hence, we have proved Eq. (3.4) and also the theorem.  □\Box

Corollary 3.2.

For any λ⁡(ξ)∈ℂ⁡[ξ]\lambda(\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi] and p⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]p(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], we have

(3.8) ℛ⁡(λ⁡(∂)​p​(z))\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda(\partial)p(z)) =λ⁡(ξ)∗t=−1p⁡(z).\displaystyle=\lambda(\xi)\ast_{t=-1}p(z).
(3.9) ℒ⁡(p⁡(z)​λ​(∂))\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}(p(z)\lambda(\partial)) =λ⁡(ξ)∗p⁡(z).\displaystyle=\lambda(\xi)\ast p(z).

Proof:  By Eqs. (3.2) and (2.20) with t=1t=1, we have

ℛ⁡(λ⁡(∂)​p​(z))\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda(\partial)p(z)) =ℛ⁡(ℒ−1​(λ⁡(ξ)​p​(z)))=(ℛ∘ℒ−1)​(λ⁡(ξ)​p​(z))\displaystyle={\mathcal{R}}({\mathcal{L}}^{-1}(\lambda(\xi)p(z)))=({\mathcal{R}}\circ{\mathcal{L}}^{-1})(\lambda(\xi)p(z))
=Φt=1​(λ⁡(ξ)​p​(z))=λ⁡(ξ)∗t=−1p⁡(z).\displaystyle=\Phi_{t=1}(\lambda(\xi)p(z))=\lambda(\xi)\ast_{t=-1}p(z).

So we have Eq. (3.8). Eq. (3.9) can be proved similarly by using Eqs. (3.3) and (2.20) with t=−1t=-1.  □\Box

Finally, we end this section with the following one-variable example.

Example 3.3.

Let n=1n=1 and ϕ=z2∂3\phi=z^{2}\partial^{3}. Then,

ℛ⁡(ϕ)\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}(\phi) =ℛ(z2∂3)=ξ3z2.\displaystyle={\mathcal{R}}(z^{2}\partial^{3})=\xi^{3}z^{2}.
ℒ⁡(ϕ)\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}(\phi) =ℒ(z2∂3)=ξ3∗z2=(z−δ)2ξ3\displaystyle={\mathcal{L}}(z^{2}\partial^{3})=\xi^{3}\ast z^{2}=(z-\delta)^{2}\xi^{3}
=(z2−2​z​δ+δ2)​ξ3=ξ3​z2−6​ξ2​z+6​ξ.\displaystyle=(z^{2}-2z\delta+\delta^{2})\xi^{3}=\xi^{3}z^{2}-6\xi^{2}z+6\xi.

Therefore, we have

ϕ=z2∂3=∂3z2−6∂2z+6∂.\displaystyle\phi=z^{2}\partial^{3}=\partial^{3}z^{2}-6\partial^{2}z+6\partial.

4. A Re-formulation of the Image Conjecture on Commuting Differential Operators of Order One with Constant Leading Coefficients

In this section, we show that the algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}) is closely related with a theorem (See Theorem 4.1) first proved in [Z3] and also with the so-called image conjecture (See Conjecture 4.3) proposed in [Z3] on the differential operators ξ−t∂\xi-t\partial (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}).

In Subsection 4.1, we use certain Taylor series expansion of elements of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] to give a new and more conceptual proof for Theorem 4.1. In Subsection 4.2, we first give a new formulation (See Conjecture 4.5) for Conjecture 4.3 in terms of the algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] and the notion of Mathieu subspaces (see Definition 4.2) introduced in [Z4], and then show in Theorem 4.6 that the new formulation is indeed equivalent to Conjecture 4.3.

4.1. The Taylor Series with Respect to the Product ∗t\ast_{t}

First, let us recall the following elementary fact on polynomials in ξ\xi and zz.

For any f⁡(ξ,z)∈𝒜⁡[ξ,z]f({\xi,z})\in{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}], we may view f⁡(ξ,z)f({\xi,z}) as a polynomial in ξ\xi with coefficients in 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z]. Then it has the following Taylor series expansion

(4.1) f⁡(ξ,z)=∑α∈ℕn1α!​ξα​cα​(z)\displaystyle f({\xi,z})=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{1}{\alpha!}\,\,\xi^{\alpha}c_{\alpha}(z)

for some cα​(z)∈𝒜​[z]c_{\alpha}(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z].

Let ev0:𝒜[ξ,z]→𝒜[z]ev_{{}_{0}}:{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[z] be the evaluation map of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] at ξ=0\xi=0, i.e. for any u⁡(ξ,z)∈𝒜⁡[ξ,z]u({\xi,z})\in{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}], ev0(u):=u(0,z)ev_{{}_{0}}(u)\!:=u(0,z). Then, the cα​(z)c_{\alpha}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) in Eq. (4.1) are given by

(4.2) cα(z)=ev0(δαf).\displaystyle c_{\alpha}(z)=ev_{{}_{0}}(\delta^{\alpha}f).

Note that another characterization of the evaluation map ev0ev_{{}_{0}} is that ev0ev_{{}_{0}} is the (unique) algebra homomorphism from 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] to 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] with ev0(ξi)=0ev_{{}_{0}}(\xi_{i})=0 and ev0(zi)=ziev_{{}_{0}}(z_{i})=z_{i} for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Now, come back to our algebras ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}). By Proposition 2.6, (c)(c), we know that ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] is also a commutative free algebra generated freely by ξ\xi and zz with the same base vector space ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]. Hence, we should expect similar expansions as in Eq. (4.1) for polynomials f⁡(ξ,z)∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]f({\xi,z})\in\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] with respect to the product ∗t\ast_{t}.

But, in order to formulate the expected expansions precisely, we need first to introduce the analogue of the evaluation map ev0ev_{{}_{0}} for the algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

Note that, by Proposition 2.6, (b)(b), the subalgebra of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] generated by zz is also 𝒜⁡[z]⊂ℂ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z]\subset\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}]. Parallel to the second characterization of the evaluation map ev0ev_{{}_{0}} mentioned above, we let ℰt{\mathcal{E}}_{t} be the unique algebra homomorphism from ℬt​[ξ,z]→𝒜​[z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[z] such that ℰt​(ξi)=0{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(\xi_{i})=0 and ℰt​(zi)=zi{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(z_{i})=z_{i} for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Note also that, by Eqs. (2.18) and (2.19), the algebra isomorphism Φt:ℬt​[ξ,z]→𝒜⁡[ξ,z]\Phi_{t}:{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] maps ξi\xi_{i} (resp. ziz_{i}) to ξi\xi_{i} (resp. ziz_{i}) for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Hence the composition ev0∘Φt:ℬt[ξ,z]→𝒜[z]ev_{{}_{0}}\circ\Phi_{t}:{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[z] has the same characterizing property of ℰt{\mathcal{E}}_{t}. Therefore, we have

(4.3) ℰt=ev0∘Φt.\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t}=ev_{{}_{0}}\circ\Phi_{t}.

Furthermore, we can also derive a more explicit formula for ℰt{\mathcal{E}}_{t} as follows.

For any α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and p⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]p(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z], consider

(4.4) ℰt​(ξα​p​(z))\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(\xi^{\alpha}p(z)) =ev0(Φt(ξαp(z)))\displaystyle=ev_{{}_{0}}(\Phi_{t}(\xi^{\alpha}p(z)))
Applying Eq. (2.20) and then Eq. (2.14) with tt replaced by −t-t:
=ev0(ξα∗−tp(z)))\displaystyle=ev_{{}_{0}}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{-t}p(z)))
=ev0((ξ+t∂)α(p(z)))=t|α|∂α(p(z)).\displaystyle=ev_{{}_{0}}((\xi+t\partial)^{\alpha}(p(z)))=t^{|\alpha|}\partial^{\alpha}(p(z)).

From the formula above, we see that, for any g⁡(z,ξ)∈ℂ⁡[z,ξ]g(z,\xi)\in\mathbb{C}[z,\xi], ℰt​(g⁡(z,ξ))∈ℂ⁡[z]{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(g(z,\xi))\in\mathbb{C}[z] can be obtained by, first, writing each monomial of g⁡(z,ξ)g(z,\xi) as ξβ​zγ\xi^{\beta}z^{\gamma} (β,γ∈ℕn)(\beta,\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}), i.e. putting the free variables ξi\xi_{i}’s to the most left in each monomial of g⁡(z,ξ)g(z,\xi), and then replacing the part ξβ\xi^{\beta} by the differential operator t|β|∂βt^{|\beta|}\partial^{\beta} and applying it to the other part zγz^{\gamma} of the monomial. For examples, we have

ℰt​(1)\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(1) =1;\displaystyle=1;
ℰt​(zα)\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(z^{\alpha}) =(t∂)0(zα)=zαfor any α∈ℕn;\displaystyle=(t\partial)^{0}(z^{\alpha})=z^{\alpha}\qquad\quad\,\,\qquad\qquad\mbox{for any }\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n};
ℰt​(ξα)\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(\xi^{\alpha}) =t|α|​∂α(1)=0for any ​0≠α∈ℕn;\displaystyle=t^{|\alpha|}\partial^{\alpha}(1)=0\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\quad\mbox{for any }0\neq\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n};
ℰt​(z1m​ξ12)\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t}(z_{1}^{m}\xi_{1}^{2}) =t2​∂12(z1m)=m⁡(m−1)​t2​z1m−2for any ​m≥2.\displaystyle=t^{2}\partial_{1}^{2}(z_{1}^{m})=m(m-1)t^{2}z_{1}^{m-2}\qquad\,\mbox{for any }m\geq 2.

Now we are ready to formulate and prove the expected expansion of polynomials with respect to the new product ∗t\ast_{t}, which is parallel to the Taylor expansion in Eq. (4.1).

Theorem 4.1.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} and f⁡(ξ,z)∈ℂ⁡[ξ,z]f(\xi,z)\in\mathbb{C}[\xi,z], we have

(4.5) f⁡(ξ,z)\displaystyle f(\xi,z) =∑α∈ℕn1α!​ξα∗taα​(z),\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{1}{\alpha!}\,\,\xi^{\alpha}\ast_{t}a_{\alpha}(z),
(4.6) f⁡(ξ,z)\displaystyle f(\xi,z) =∑α∈ℕn1α!(ξ−t∂z)αaα(z),\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{1}{\alpha!}\,(\xi-t\partial_{z})^{\alpha}a_{\alpha}(z),

where, for any α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n},

(4.7) aα​(z)=ℰt​(δα​f).\displaystyle a_{\alpha}(z)={\mathcal{E}}_{t}(\delta^{\alpha}f).

Furthermore, the expansions of the forms in Eqs. (4.5)(\ref{D_t-Taylor-e1}) and (4.6)(\ref{D_t-Taylor-e2}) for f⁡(ξ,z)f({\xi,z}) are unique.

Proof:  Note first that, by Eq. (2.14) in Proposition 2.4, Eq. (4.5) and Eq. (4.6) are actually equivalent. So we will focus only on Eq. (4.5).

The uniqueness of the expansion in Eq. (4.5) follows directly from Proposition 2.6, (a)(a)-(c)(c).

To show that Eq. (4.5) with aα​(z)a_{\alpha}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) given in Eq. (4.7) does hold, we first write the Taylor series expansion of Φt​(f​(ξ,z))\Phi_{t}(f({\xi,z})) as in Eq. (4.1):

(4.8) Φt​(f⁡(ξ,z))=∑α∈ℕn1α!​ξα​aα​(z)\displaystyle\Phi_{t}(f({\xi,z}))=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{1}{\alpha!}\,\,\xi^{\alpha}a_{\alpha}(z)

where aα​(z)∈ℂ​[z]a_{\alpha}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) are given by

(4.9) aα(z)=ev0(δαΦt(f)).\displaystyle a_{\alpha}(z)=ev_{{}_{0}}(\delta^{\alpha}\Phi_{t}(f)).

Applying Φ−t\Phi_{-t} to Eq.(4.8) and, by Eq. (2.20) with tt replaced by −t-t, we get Eq. (4.5).

Next, note that δα\delta^{\alpha} (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) commute with Λ\Lambda, hence they also commute with Φt=et​Λ\Phi_{t}=e^{t\Lambda}. Then, by Eqs. (4.9) and (4.3), we have

aα(z)=ev0(Φt(δαf))=(ev0∘Φt)(δαf)=ℰt(δαf).\displaystyle a_{\alpha}(z)=ev_{{}_{0}}(\Phi_{t}(\delta^{\alpha}f))=(ev_{{}_{0}}\circ\Phi_{t})(\delta^{\alpha}f)={\mathcal{E}}_{t}(\delta^{\alpha}f).

Therefore, Eq. (4.7) also holds.  □\Box

Several remarks on Theorem 4.1 and the proof above are as follows.

First, Theorem 4.1 with t=1t=1 was first proved in [Z3]. The proof in [Z3] is more straightforward. It does not use the algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] and the product ∗t\ast_{t}. But the proof given here is more conceptual. For example, the expansion in Eq. (4.6)(\ref{D_t-Taylor-e2}) becomes much more natural after we show here that it is just the usual Taylor series expansion of polynomials as in Eq. (4.1)(\ref{Taylor-e1}) but in the new context of the algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

Second, Eq. (4.7) can also be derived directly from Eq. (4.6) as in [Z3]. Namely, apply δα\delta^{\alpha} to Eq. (4.6) and then replace ξ\xi by t∂t\partial in both sides of the resulting equation.

Third, not all formal power series f⁡(ξ,z)∈𝒜⁡[[ξ,z]]f({\xi,z})\in{\mathcal{A}}[[{\xi,z}]] can be expanded in the form of Eq. (4.5)(\ref{D_t-Taylor-e1}) or (4.6)(\ref{D_t-Taylor-e2}). For example, let n=1n=1 and f⁡(ξ,z)=eξ​zf({\xi,z})=e^{\xi z} and assume that (4.6)(\ref{D_t-Taylor-e2}) holds for f⁡(ξ,z)f({\xi,z}). Then, by the argument in the previous paragraph, we see that am​(z)a_{m}(z) (m≥0)(m\geq 0) must be given by Eq. (4.7). But, for the series δm​f​(ξ,z)=zm​∑k≥0(ξ​z)kk!\delta^{m}f({\xi,z})=z^{m}\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{(\xi z)^{k}}{k!}, ℰt{\mathcal{E}}_{t} is not well-defined, which is a contradiction.

Another way to look at the fact above is as follows. Even though ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t≠0)(t\neq 0) and 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] share the same base vector space ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z], by Proposition 2.9, we know that they induce different ℓ\ell-adic topologies on ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]. Therefore, their completions with respect to the different ℓ\ell-adic topologies will be different. In other words, the formal power series algebras with respect to the product ∗t\ast_{t} (t≠0)(t\neq 0) and the usual formal power series algebra 𝒜⁡[[ξ,z]]{\mathcal{A}}[[{\xi,z}]] do not share the same base vector space anymore.

For the example f⁡(ξ,z)=eξ​zf({\xi,z})=e^{\xi z} above, we have f⁡(ξ,z)∈𝒜⁡[[ξ,z]]f({\xi,z})\in{\mathcal{A}}[[{\xi,z}]]. But, by the argument in the proof of Proposition 2.9 with αm\alpha_{m} (m≥1)(m\geq 1) replaced by mm, it is easy to see that, for any t≠0t\neq 0, f⁡(ξ,z)=eξ​zf({\xi,z})=e^{\xi z} does not lie in the completion of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] with respect to the ℓ\ell-adic topology on ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] induced by ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]. Therefore, f⁡(ξ,z)=eξ​zf({\xi,z})=e^{\xi z} can not be written as a formal power series with respect to the product ∗t\ast_{t} as in Eq. (4.5).

4.2. Re-Formulation of the Image Conjecture in Terms of the Algebra ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}]

First let us recall the following notion introduced recently in [Z4].

Definition 4.2.

Let RR be any commutative ring and 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} a commutative RR-algebra. We say that an RR-subspace ℳ{\mathcal{M}} of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} if the following property holds: if a∈𝒜a\in{\mathcal{A}} satisfies am∈ℳa^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for all m≥1m\geq 1, then, for any b∈𝒜b\in{\mathcal{A}}, we have b​am∈ℳba^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for all m≫0m\gg 0, i.e. there exists N≥1N\geq 1 ((depending on aa and bb)) such that b​am∈ℳba^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for all m≥Nm\geq N.

From the definition above, it is easy to see that any ideal of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is automatically a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, but not conversely (See [Z4] for some examples of Mathieu subspaces which are not ideals). Therefore, the notion of Mathieu subspaces can be viewed as a generalization of the notion of ideals.

Next, for any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, set

(4.10) Im(ξ−t∂):=∑i=1n(ξi−t∂i)ℂ[ξ,z].\displaystyle\rm{Im\,}(\xi-t\partial)\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\xi_{i}-t\partial_{i})\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}].

We call Im(ξ−t∂)\rm{Im\,}(\xi-t\partial) the image of the commuting differential operators (ξi−t∂i)(\xi_{i}-t\partial_{i}) (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).

With the notion and notation fixed above, the image conjecture proposed in [Z4] for the commuting differential operators (ξ−t∂)(\xi-t\partial) can be re-stated as follows.

Conjecture 4.3.

For any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, Im(ξ−t∂)\rm{Im\,}(\xi-t\partial) is a Mathieu subspace of the polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}].

One of the motivations of the conjecture above is the following theorem proved in [Z3].

Theorem 4.4.

Conjecture 4.3 implies the Jacobian conjecture.

Actually, it has been shown in [Z3] that the Jacobian conjecture is equivalent to some very special cases of Conjecture 4.3. For more detail, see [Z3].

The main result of this subsection is to show that the conjecture above can actually be re-formulated as follows.

Conjecture 4.5.

Set ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]:=∑i=1mξi​ℂ​[ξ,z]\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}]\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\xi_{i}\mathbb{C}[\xi,z]. Then, for any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] as a subspace of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] is a Mathieu subspace of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

Theorem 4.6.

Conjecture 4.5 is equivalent to Conjecture 4.3.

Proof:  First, denote by ξ∗tℂ⁡[ξ,z]\xi\ast_{t}\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] the ideal of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] generated by ξi\xi_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). View ξ∗tℂ⁡[ξ,z]\xi\ast_{t}\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] as a subspace of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] and apply Eqs. (4.10) and (2.14), we have

(4.11) Im(ξ−t∂)=∑i=1nξi∗tℂ[ξ,z]=ξ∗tℂ[ξ,z].\displaystyle\rm{Im\,}(\xi-t\partial)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}\ast_{t}\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}]=\xi\ast_{t}\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}].

Second, by Eqs. (2.1) and (2.18), we have

Φt​(ξ∗tℂ⁡[ξ,z])=Φt​(ξ)​Φt​(ℂ⁡[ξ,z])=ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]\displaystyle\Phi_{t}(\xi\ast_{t}\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}])=\Phi_{t}(\xi)\Phi_{t}(\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}])=\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}]

Hence, we also have

(4.12) ξ∗tℂ⁡[ξ,z]=Φt−1​(ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z])=Φ−t​(ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]).\displaystyle\xi\ast_{t}\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}]=\Phi_{t}^{-1}(\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}])=\Phi_{-t}(\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}]).

Combine Eqs. (4.11) and (4.12), we get

(4.13) Φ−t(ξℂ[ξ,z])=Im(ξ−t∂).\displaystyle\Phi_{-t}(\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}])=\rm{Im\,}(\xi-t\partial).

Third, by Proposition 4.94.9 in [Z4], we know that pre-images of Mathieu subspaces under algebra homomorphisms are still Mathieu subspaces, from which it is easy to check that Mathieu subspaces are preserved by algebra isomorphisms. By using this fact (on the algebra isomorphism Φ−t:ℬ−t​[ξ,z]→𝒜⁡[ξ,z]\Phi_{-t}:{\mathcal{B}}_{-t}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}]) and also Eq. (4.13), we see that, ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] is a Mathieu subspace of ℬ−t​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{-t}[{\xi,z}] iff Im(ξ−t∂)\rm{Im\,}(\xi-t\partial) is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}].

Replacing tt by −t-t in the equivalence above, we have that, ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] is a Mathieu subspace of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] for any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} iff Im(ξ+t∂)\rm{Im\,}(\xi+t\partial) is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] for any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} iff Im(ξ−t∂)\rm{Im\,}(\xi-t\partial) is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] for any t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}. Hence, we have proved the theorem.  □\Box

From Theorems 4.4 and 4.6, we immediately have the following corollary.

Corollary 4.7.

Conjecture 4.5 implies the Jacobian conjecture.

Remark 4.8.

Note that, when t=0t=0, Conjecture 4.5 is trivial since ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]\xi\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] is an ideal of the algebra ℬt=0​[ξ,z]=𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t=0}[{\xi,z}]={\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}]. In general, Conjecture 4.5 in some sense just claims that the algebras ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}) do not differ or change too much from 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] so that the vector subspace ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]\xi\mathbb{C}[\xi,z] still remains as a Mathieu subspace of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}].

From this point of view, the triviality of the deformation ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] (t∈ℂ)(t\in\mathbb{C}) of the polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] given in Corollary 2.2 may be viewed as a fact in favor of Conjecture 4.5, hence also to the Jacobian conjecture via the implication in Corollary 4.7.

Remark 4.9.

Conjecture 4.5 and also the Jacobian conjecture can be viewed as problems caused by the following fact. Namely, due to the change of the algebra structure from 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] to ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}], the evaluation map at ξ=0\xi=0, which is an algebra homomorphism from 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] to 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z], is not an algebra homomorphism from ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] to 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] if t≠0t\neq 0. Therefore, its kernel ξ​ℂ​[ξ,z]\xi\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] does not remain to be an ideal of ℬt​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}_{t}[{\xi,z}] anymore.

But, on the other hand, as we will see later in Subsection 5.2 ((See Theorem 5.2 and Remark 5.4)), the same fact for the evaluation map at ξ=1\xi=1, i.e. ξi=1\xi_{i}=1 (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), in some sense also causes something truely remarkable, namely, the generalized Laguerre polynomials.

5. Connections with the Generalized Laguerre Polynomials

In this section, we study some connections and interactions of the monomials of the algebra ℬ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}[{\xi,z}] in ξ\xi and zz with the generalized Laguerre polynomials in one or more variables.

In Subsection 5.1, we briefly recall the definition and the orthogonal property of the generalized Laguerre polynomials. In Subsection 5.2, we show that the generalized Laguerre polynomials can be obtained from certain monomials of the algebra ℬ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}[{\xi,z}] in ξ\xi and zz (See Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.3).

In Subsection 5.3, we study some applications of the connection given in Theorem 5.2. We first use certain properties of the generalized Laguerre polynomials to derive some results on some monomials of ℬ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}[{\xi,z}] in ξ\xi and zz. We then use some results derived in Section 2 on the algebra ℬ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}[{\xi,z}] to give new proofs for some important properties of the generalized Laguerre polynomials (see Proposition 5.11 and Theorem 5.12).

5.1. The Generalized Laguerre Orthogonal Polynomials

First, let us recall the generalized Laguerre orthogonal polynomials in one variable.

For any k∈ℝk\in{\mathbb{R}} and m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}, the generalized Laguerre polynomial Lm[k]​(z)L_{m}^{[k]}(z) in one variable is given by

(5.1) Lm[k]​(z)=∑j=0m(m+km−j)​(−z)jj!.\displaystyle L_{m}^{[k]}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\binom{m+k}{m-j}\,\frac{(-z)^{j}}{j!}.

Here we are only interested in the case that k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. For any fixed k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, the generating function of the generalized Laguerre polynomials Lm[k]​(z)L_{m}^{[k]}(z) (m≥0)(m\geq 0) is given by

(5.2) exp⁡(−z​u1−u)(1−u)k+1=∑m=0+∞Lm[k]​(z)​um,\displaystyle\frac{\exp(-\frac{zu}{1-u})}{(1-u)^{k+1}}=\sum_{m=0}^{+\infty}L_{m}^{[k]}(z)\,u^{m},

where uu above denotes a formal variable which commutes with zz.

The multi-variable generalized Laguerre polynomials are defined as follows.

Let 𝐤=(k1,k2,…,kn)∈ℕn{\bf k}=(k_{1},k_{2},...,k_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn{\alpha}=(a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}. The generalized Laguerre polynomials in nn-variable z=(z1,z2,…,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},...,z_{n}) is defined by

(5.3) Lα[𝐤](z):=La1[k1](z1)La2[k2](z2)⋯Lan[kn](zn).\displaystyle L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(z)\!:=L_{a_{1}}^{[k_{1}]}(z_{1})L_{a_{2}}^{[k_{2}]}(z_{2})\cdots L_{a_{n}}^{[k_{n}]}(z_{n}).

The polynomials Lα​(z):=Lα[0]​(z)L_{\alpha}(z)\!:=L_{\alpha}^{[0]}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) are the so-called the (classical) Laguerre polynomials. They were named after Edmond. N. Laguerre [L]. The generalized Laguerre polynomials were introduced much later by G. Pólya and G. Szegö [PS] in 19761976.

One of the most important properties of the generalized Laguerre polynomials is the following theorem.

Theorem 5.1.

For any 𝐤,α,β∈ℕn{\bf k},\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(5.4) ∫(ℝ>0)nLα[𝐤]​(z)​Lβ[𝐤]​(z)​w​(z)​𝑑z=δα,β​(α+𝐤)!α!,\displaystyle\int_{({\mathbb{R}}_{>0})^{n}}L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(z)L_{\beta}^{[{\bf k}]}(z)\,w(z)\,dz=\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,\frac{(\alpha+{\bf k})!}{\alpha!},

where δα,β\delta_{\alpha,\beta} is the Kronecker delta function and w⁡(z)w(z) given by

(5.5) w(z):=z𝐤e−∑i=1nzi.\displaystyle w(z)\!:=z^{\bf k}e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}}.

The function w⁡(z)w(z) above is called the weight function of the generalized Laguerre polynomials Lα[𝐤]​(z)L_{\alpha}^{[\bf k]}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}).

Consequently, with any fixed 𝐤{\bf k}, the generalized Laguerre polynomials Lα[𝐤]​(z)L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) form an orthogonal basis of ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] with respect to the Hermitian form defined by

(5.6) (f,g)=∫(ℝ>0)nf⁡(z)​g¯​(z)​w​(z)​𝑑z,\displaystyle(f,g)=\int_{({\mathbb{R}}_{>0})^{n}}f(z)\bar{g}(z)\,w(z)\,dz,

where g¯​(z)\bar{g}(z) denotes the complex conjugation of the polynomial g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z].

There are many other interesting and important properties of the generalized Laguerre polynomials. We refer the reader to [Sz], [PS], [AAR] and [DX] for very thorough study on this family of orthogonal polynomials. See also the Wolfram Research web sources [W1] and [W2] for over one hundred formulas and identities on the (generalized) Laguerre polynomials.

5.2. The Generalized Laguerre Polynomials in Terms of the Product ∗\ast

The main result of this subsection is the following theorem.

Theorem 5.2.

For any 𝐤,α∈ℕn{\bf k},\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(5.7) Lα[𝐤]​(ξ​z)\displaystyle L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(\xi z) =(−1)|α|α!​ξ−𝐤​(ξα+𝐤∗zα).\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\,\xi^{-{\bf k}}(\xi^{\alpha+{\bf k}}\ast z^{\alpha}).
(5.8) Lα[𝐤]​(ξ​z)\displaystyle L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(\xi z) =(−1)|α|α!​z−𝐤​(ξα∗zα+𝐤),\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\,z^{-{\bf k}}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+{\bf k}}),

where ξ​z:=(ξ1​z1,ξ2​z2,…,ξn​zn)\xi z\!:=(\xi_{1}z_{1},\xi_{2}z_{2},...,\xi_{n}z_{n}).

In particular, for the Laguerre polynomials, we have

(5.9) Lα​(ξ​z)=(−1)|α|α!​ξα∗zα.\displaystyle L_{\alpha}(\xi z)=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\,\,\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha}.

Proof:  We first prove Eq. (5.9). Note first that, as pointed out in Subsection 2.12.1 [Z4], the Laguerre polynomials Lm​(z)L_{m}(z) (m∈ℕ)(m\in{\mathbb{N}}) in one variable can be obtained as

(5.10) Lm(z)=1m!(∂−1)m(zm).\displaystyle L_{m}(z)=\frac{1}{m!}(\partial-1)^{m}(z^{m}).

Changing the variable z→ξ​zz\to\xi z in the equation above, we get

Lm​(ξ​z)\displaystyle L_{m}(\xi z) =1m!(ξ−1∂−1)m(ξmzm)=1m!ξ−m(∂−ξ)m(ξmzm)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m!}(\xi^{-1}\partial-1)^{m}(\xi^{m}z^{m})=\frac{1}{m!}\xi^{-m}(\partial-\xi)^{m}(\xi^{m}z^{m})
=1m!(∂−ξ)m(zm)=(−1)mm!(ξ−∂)m(zm).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m!}(\partial-\xi)^{m}(z^{m})=\frac{(-1)^{m}}{m!}(\xi-\partial)^{m}(z^{m}).

By Eq. (5.3) with 𝐤=0{\bf k}=0 and the equation above, we see that the multi-variable Laguerre polynomials Lα​(z)L_{\alpha}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) can be given by

(5.11) Lα(ξz)=(−1)|α|α!(ξ−∂)α(zα).\displaystyle L_{\alpha}(\xi z)=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}(\xi-\partial)^{\alpha}(z^{\alpha}).

Then, apply Eq. (2.14) with λ⁡(ξ)=ξα\lambda(\xi)=\xi^{\alpha} and t=1t=1, we get Eq. (5.9).

To show Eq. (5.7), recall that we have the following well-known identity for the one-variable generalized Laguerre polynomials, which can be easily derived from the generating functions of the generalized Laguerre polynomials in Eq. (5.2):

(5.12) Lm[k]​(z)=(−1)k​∂kLm+k​(z).\displaystyle L_{m}^{[k]}(z)=(-1)^{k}\partial^{k}L_{m+k}(z).

Now, by Eq. (5.3) and the equation above, we see that the multi-variable generalized Laguerre polynomials can be given by

(5.13) Lα[𝐤]​(z)=(−1)|𝐤|​∂𝐤Lα+𝐤​(z).\displaystyle L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(z)=(-1)^{|\bf k|}\partial^{\bf k}L_{\alpha+{\bf k}}(z).

Changing the variable z→ξ​zz\to\xi z in the equation above, we get

(5.14) Lα[𝐤]​(ξ​z)\displaystyle L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(\xi z) =(−1)|𝐤|​(∂𝐤Lα+𝐤)​(ξ​z)\displaystyle=(-1)^{|\bf k|}(\partial^{\bf k}L_{\alpha+{\bf k}})(\xi z)
=(−1)|𝐤|​ξ−𝐤​∂𝐤(Lα+𝐤​(ξ​z))\displaystyle=(-1)^{|\bf k|}\xi^{-{\bf k}}\partial^{\bf k}(L_{\alpha+{\bf k}}(\xi z))
Applying Eq. (5.9) and then Eq.(2.29):
=(−1)|α|(α+𝐤)!​ξ−𝐤​∂𝐤(ξα+𝐤∗zα+𝐤).\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{(\alpha+{\bf k})!}\xi^{-{\bf k}}\partial^{\bf k}(\xi^{\alpha+{\bf k}}\ast z^{\alpha+{\bf k}}).
=(−1)|α|α!​ξ−𝐤​(ξα+𝐤∗zα).\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\xi^{-{\bf k}}(\xi^{\alpha+{\bf k}}\ast z^{\alpha}).

Hence, we get Eq. (5.7). Switching ξ\xi and zz in Eq. (5.7) and using the commutativity of the product ∗\ast, we get Eq. (5.8).  □\Box

Corollary 5.3.

For any 𝐤,α∈ℕn{\bf k},\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

Lα​(z)\displaystyle L_{\alpha}(z) =(−1)|α|α!​(ξα∗zα)|ξ=1;\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\,\,\left.(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha})\right|_{\xi=1};
Lα[𝐤]​(z)\displaystyle L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(z) =(−1)|α|α!​(ξα+𝐤∗zα)|ξ=1;\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\,\left.(\xi^{\alpha+{\bf k}}\ast z^{\alpha})\right|_{\xi=1};
Lα[𝐤]​(z)\displaystyle L_{\alpha}^{[{\bf k}]}(z) =(−1)|α|α!​z−𝐤​(ξα∗zα+𝐤)|ξ=1,\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\,\left.z^{-{\bf k}}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+{\bf k}})\right|_{\xi=1},

where |ξ=1|_{{}_{\xi=1}} denotes the evaluation map from ℂ⁡[ξ,z]\mathbb{C}[{\xi,z}] to ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] by setting ξi=1\xi_{i}=1 for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Remark 5.4.

Note that, the evaluation map |ξ=1|_{{}_{\xi=1}} viewed as a linear map from 𝒜⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}[{\xi,z}] to 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] is a homomorphism of algebras. But, as a linear map from the algebra ℬ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}[{\xi,z}] to the polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z], it is not a homomorphism of algebras anymore. In particular, we have

(ξα∗zα)|ξ=1≠1∗zα=zα.\displaystyle\left.(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha})\right|_{\xi=1}\neq 1\ast z^{\alpha}=z^{\alpha}.

Otherwise the generalized Laguerre polynomials would be trivialized.

Therefore, in some sense, the fact that the evaluation map |ξ=1:ℬ[ξ,z]→𝒜[z]|_{{}_{\xi=1}}:{\mathcal{B}}[{\xi,z}]\to{\mathcal{A}}[z] fails to be an algebra homomorphism causes the non-trivial, actually truly remarkable, generalized Laguerre polynomials. But, on the other hand, as we have discussed in Subsection 4.2 ((See Remark 4.9)), the same fact for the evaluation map at ξ=0\xi=0 also causes some extremely difficult open problems such as Conjecture 4.5 and the Jacobian conjecture.

Another immediate consequence of Theorem 5.2 is the following corollary.

Corollary 5.5.

For any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(5.15) ξβ​(ξα∗zα+β)=zβ​(ξα+β∗zα).\displaystyle\xi^{\beta}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta})=z^{\beta}(\xi^{\alpha+\beta}\ast z^{\alpha}).

Note that the corollary follows immediately from Eqs. (5.7) and (5.8) with 𝐤=β{\bf k}=\beta. But here we also give a more straightforward proof.

Proof:  Consider

ξβ​(ξα∗zα+β)\displaystyle\xi^{\beta}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta}) =(ξ−∂+∂)β(ξα∗zα+β)\displaystyle=(\xi-\partial+\partial)^{\beta}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta})
=∑γ∈ℕn(βγ)(ξ−∂)β−γ∂γ(ξα∗zα+β)\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\binom{\beta}{\gamma}(\xi-\partial)^{\beta-\gamma}\partial^{\gamma}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta})
Applying Eq. (2.29) and then Eq.(2.14):
=∑γ∈ℕn(βγ)(α+β)!(α+β−γ)!(ξ−∂)β−γ(ξα∗zα+β−γ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\binom{\beta}{\gamma}\frac{(\alpha+\beta)!}{(\alpha+\beta-\gamma)!}\,(\xi-\partial)^{\beta-\gamma}(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta-\gamma})
=∑γ∈ℕn(βγ)​(α+β)!(α+β−γ)!​ξβ−γ∗(ξα∗zα+β−γ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\binom{\beta}{\gamma}\frac{(\alpha+\beta)!}{(\alpha+\beta-\gamma)!}\,\xi^{\beta-\gamma}\ast(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta-\gamma})
=∑γ∈ℕnβ(βγ)​(α+β)!(α+β−γ)!​(ξα+β−γ∗zα+β−γ).\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}^{\beta}\binom{\beta}{\gamma}\frac{(\alpha+\beta)!}{(\alpha+\beta-\gamma)!}\,(\xi^{\alpha+\beta-\gamma}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta-\gamma}).

By switching ξ↔z\xi\leftrightarrow z in the argument above and using the commutativity of the product ∗\ast, it is easy to see that we also have

zβ​(ξα+β∗zα)=∑γ∈ℕnβ(βγ)​(α+β)!(α+β−γ)!​(ξα+β−γ∗zα+β−γ).\displaystyle z^{\beta}(\xi^{\alpha+\beta}\ast z^{\alpha})=\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}^{\beta}\binom{\beta}{\gamma}\frac{(\alpha+\beta)!}{(\alpha+\beta-\gamma)!}\,(\xi^{\alpha+\beta-\gamma}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta-\gamma}).

Hence Eq. (5.15) follows.  □\Box

5.3. Some Applications of Theorem 5.2

First, let us derive some identities for the exponential series exp∗⁡(⋅)=e∗{⋅}\exp_{*}(\cdot)=e_{\ast}^{\{\cdot\}} of the algebra ℬ⁡[ξ,z]{\mathcal{B}}[{\xi,z}], i.e. the usual exponential series but with the product replaced by ∗\ast.

Proposition 5.6.

Let u=(u1,u2,…,un)u=(u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{n}) be nn free commutative variables. Set ξ∗z:=(ξ1∗z1,ξ2∗z2,…,ξn∗zn)\xi\ast z\!:=(\xi_{1}\ast z_{1},\,\xi_{2}\ast z_{2},...,\,\xi_{n}\ast z_{n}) and (ξ∗z)​u:=∑i=1n(ξi∗zi)​ui(\xi\ast z)u\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\xi_{i}\ast z_{i})u_{i}. Then, for any 𝐤=(k1,k2,…,kn)∈ℕn{\bf k}=(k_{1},k_{2},...,k_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(5.16) ξ−𝐤​(ξ𝐤∗e∗−(ξ∗z)​u)\displaystyle\xi^{-\bf k}\left(\xi^{\bf k}\ast e_{*}^{-(\xi\ast z)u}\right) =∏i=1nexp⁡(−(ξi​zi)​ui1−ui)(1−ui)ki+1.\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\,\,\frac{\exp(-\,\frac{(\xi_{i}z_{i})\,u_{i}}{1-u_{i}})}{(1-u_{i})^{k_{i}+1}}.
(5.17) z−𝐤​(z𝐤∗e∗−(ξ∗z)​u)\displaystyle z^{-\bf k}\left(z^{\bf k}\ast e_{*}^{-(\xi\ast z)u}\right) =∏i=1nexp⁡(−(ξi​zi)​ui1−ui)(1−ui)ki+1.\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\,\,\frac{\exp(-\,\frac{(\xi_{i}z_{i})\,u_{i}}{1-u_{i}})}{(1-u_{i})^{k_{i}+1}}.

In particular, when 𝐤=0{\bf k}=0, we have the following expression of the exponential exp∗⁡(−(ξ∗z)​u)\exp_{*}(-(\xi\ast z)u):

(5.18) exp∗⁡(−(ξ∗z)​u)\displaystyle\exp_{*}(-(\xi\ast z)u) =∏i=1nexp⁡(−(ξi​zi)​ui1−ui)(1−ui).\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\,\,\frac{\exp(-\,\frac{(\xi_{i}z_{i})\,u_{i}}{1-u_{i}})}{(1-u_{i})}.

Proof:  We give a proof for Eq. (5.16). The proof of Eq. (5.17) is similar.

First, by the commutativity and associativity of the product ∗\ast and also by Proposition 2.6, (b)(b), it is easy to see that, for any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(5.19) (ξα∗zα)∗(ξβ∗zβ)\displaystyle(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha})\ast(\xi^{\beta}\ast z^{\beta}) =ξα+β∗zα+β.\displaystyle=\xi^{\alpha+\beta}\ast z^{\alpha+\beta}.
(5.20) (ξ∗z)∗α\displaystyle(\xi\ast z)^{\ast\alpha} =(ξα∗zα),\displaystyle=(\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha}),

where (ξ∗z)∗α(\xi\ast z)^{\ast\alpha} denotes the “αth\alpha^{\rm th}” power of (ξ∗z)(\xi\ast z) with respect to the new product ∗\ast.

By the last two equations above and Eq. (5.7), we have

(5.21) ξ−𝐤​(ξ𝐤∗exp∗−(ξ∗z)​u)\displaystyle\xi^{-{\bf k}}\left(\xi^{\bf k}\ast\exp_{*}^{-(\xi\ast z)u}\right) =∑α∈ℕn(−1)|α|α!​ξ−𝐤​(ξα+𝐤∗zα)​uα\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\,\xi^{-\bf k}(\xi^{\alpha+{\bf k}}\ast z^{\alpha})u^{\alpha}
=∑α∈ℕnLα[𝐤]​(ξ​z)​uα.\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}L_{\alpha}^{[\bf k]}(\xi z)u^{\alpha}.

On the other hand, by Eqs. (5.2) and (5.3), we see that the generating function of the multi-variable generalized Laguerre polynomials Lα[𝐤]​(z)L_{\alpha}^{[\bf k]}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) is given by

(5.22) ∏i=1nexp⁡(−zi​ui1−ui)(1−ui)ki+1=∑α∈ℕnLα[𝐤]​(z)​uα.\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}\,\,\frac{\exp(-\,\frac{z_{i}\,u_{i}}{1-u_{i}})}{(1-u_{i})^{k_{i}+1}}=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}L_{\alpha}^{[\bf k]}(z)u^{\alpha}.

Replacing zz by ξ​z\xi z in the equation above, we get

(5.23) ∏i=1nexp⁡(−(ξi​zi)​ui1−ui)(1−ui)ki+1=∑α∈ℕnLα[𝐤]​(ξ​z)​uα.\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}\,\,\frac{\exp(-\,\frac{(\xi_{i}z_{i})\,u_{i}}{1-u_{i}})}{(1-u_{i})^{k_{i}+1}}=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}L_{\alpha}^{[\bf k]}(\xi z)u^{\alpha}.

Combining Eqs. (5.21) and (5.23), we get Eq. (5.16).  □\Box

Next we use the connection given in Theorem 5.2 to derive more properties on the monomials in ξ\xi and zz with respect to the product ∗\ast from certain results on the generalized Laguerre polynomials.

For convenience, for any α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we set

(5.24) Lα​(z,ξ):=ξα∗zα.\displaystyle L_{\alpha}(z;\xi)\!:=\xi^{\alpha}\ast z^{\alpha}.

Note that, by Eqs. (5.1) and (5.9), the polynomials Lα​(z,ξ)L_{\alpha}(z;\xi) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) are polynomials with coefficients in ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. In particular, for any fixed ξ∈(ℝ>0)n\xi\in({\mathbb{R}}_{>0})^{n}, by Eqs. (5.1) and (5.9), it is easy to see that the polynomials Lα​(z,ξ)L_{\alpha}(z;\xi) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) are polynomials in zz with real coefficients and form a linear basis of ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z].

The next proposition says that this basis is also orthogonal with respect to the following weight function:

(5.25) wξ​(z):=e−⟨ξ,z⟩​∏i=1nξi,\displaystyle w_{\xi}(z)\!:=e^{-\langle\xi,z\rangle}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i},
Proposition 5.7.

For any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(5.26) ∫(ℝ>0)nLα​(z,ξ)​Lβ​(z,ξ)​wξ​(z)​𝑑z=(α!)2​δα,β.\displaystyle\int_{({\mathbb{R}}_{>0})^{n}}L_{\alpha}(z;\xi)L_{\beta}(z;\xi)\,w_{\xi}(z)\,dz=(\alpha!)^{2}\delta_{\alpha,\beta}.

Proof:  Note that, under the change of variables zi→ξi​ziz_{i}\to\xi_{i}z_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), by Eqs. (5.9) and (5.24) the Laguerre polynomials Lα​(z)L_{\alpha}(z) will be changed to

(5.27) Lα​(z)→Lα​(ξ​z)=(−1)|α|α!​Lα​(z,ξ).\displaystyle L_{\alpha}(z)\to L_{\alpha}(\xi z)=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}L_{\alpha}(z;\xi).

By Eq. (5.25) and also Eq. (5.5) with 𝐤=0{\bf k}=0, the weight function w⁡(z)w(z) of the Laguerre polynomials is changed to

(5.28) w⁡(z)→wξ​(z)​∏i=1nξi−1.\displaystyle w(z)\to w_{\xi}(z)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}^{-1}.

Now, apply the same changing of the variables to the integral in Eq. (5.4) with 𝐤=0{\bf k}=0, by the last two equations above, we get

(5.29) δα,β\displaystyle\delta_{\alpha,\beta} =(−1)|α+β|α!​β!​∫(ℝ>0)nLα​(z,ξ)​Lβ​(z,ξ)​wξ​(z)​𝑑z\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha+\beta|}}{\alpha!\beta!}\int_{({\mathbb{R}}_{>0})^{n}}L_{\alpha}(z;\xi)L_{\beta}(z;\xi)\,w_{\xi}(z)\,dz

Hence Eq. (5.26) follows.  □\Box

Denote by 𝒜ℚ​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{Q}}[{\xi,z}] the polynomial algebra in ξ\xi and zz over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. Next we assume n=1n=1 and consider the irreducibility of the polynomial Lα​(z,ξ)L_{\alpha}(z;\xi) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) as elements of 𝒜ℚ​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{Q}}[{\xi,z}]. But, first, we need to prove the following lemma.

Lemma 5.8.

Let ξ\xi and zz be two commutative free variables and KK any field. Then, for any f⁡(z)∈K⁡[z]f(z)\in K[z] with deg⁡f≥2\deg f\geq 2, f⁡(z)f(z) is irreducible over KK iff f⁡(ξ​z)∈K⁡[ξ,z]f(\xi z)\in K[\xi,z] ((as a polynomial in two variables)) is irreducible over KK.

Proof:  The (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part of the lemma is trivial. We use the contradiction method to show the (⇒)(\Rightarrow) part of the lemma.

Assume that f⁡(ξ​z)f(\xi z) is reducible in K⁡[ξ,z]K[{\xi,z}]. Write

(5.30) f⁡(ξ​z)=g⁡(ξ,z)​h​(ξ,z)\displaystyle f(\xi z)=g({\xi,z})h({\xi,z})

for some g⁡(ξ,z),h⁡(ξ,z)∈K⁡[ξ,z]g({\xi,z}),h({\xi,z})\in K[{\xi,z}] with deg⁡g,deg⁡h≥1\deg g,\deg h\geq 1.

Setting ξ=1\xi=1 in the equation above, we also have

(5.31) f⁡(z)=g⁡(1,z)​h​(1,z).\displaystyle f(z)=g(1,z)h(1,z).

Let K¯\bar{K} be the algebraic closure of KK. Write f⁡(z)=b​∏i=1d(z−ai)f(z)=b\prod_{i=1}^{d}(z-a_{i}) for some b∈K\{0}b\in K\backslash\{0\} and ai∈K¯a_{i}\in\bar{K} (1≤i≤d)(1\leq i\leq d). Then we have

(5.32) f⁡(ξ​z)=b​∏i=1d(ξ​z−ai).\displaystyle f(\xi z)=b\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\xi z-a_{i}).

Since f⁡(z)f(z) is irreducible over KK and deg⁡f≥2\deg f\geq 2 by the assumption, we have ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0 (1≤i≤d)(1\leq i\leq d). Hence, for each ii, ξ​z−ai\xi z-a_{i} is irreducible in K¯​[ξ,z]\bar{K}[{\xi,z}]. Then by Eqs. (5.30) and (5.32), we have

(5.33) g⁡(ξ,z)=c​∏k=1m(ξ​z−aik)\displaystyle g(\xi,z)=c\prod_{k=1}^{m}(\xi z-a_{i_{k}})

for some c∈K¯\{0}c\in\bar{K}\backslash\{0\}, 1≤m<d1\leq m<d and 1≤i1<i2<⋯<im≤d1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{m}\leq d.

However, the equation above implies g⁡(1,z)=c​∏k=1m(z−aik)g(1,z)=c\prod_{k=1}^{m}(z-a_{i_{k}}). Since g⁡(ξ,z)∈K⁡[ξ,z]g(\xi,z)\in K[{\xi,z}], we also have g⁡(1,z)∈K⁡[z]g(1,z)\in K[z]. Then by Eq. (5.31), g⁡(1,z)g(1,z) is a divisor of f⁡(z)f(z) in K⁡[z]K[z] with 1≤deg⁡g⁡(1,z)=m<d=deg⁡f⁡(z)1\leq\deg g(1,z)=m<d=\deg f(z), which contradicts to the assumption that f⁡(z)f(z) is irreducible in K⁡[z]K[z].  □\Box

Theorem 5.9.

Let ξ\xi and zz be two commutative free variables. For any m≥2m\geq 2, Lm​(z,ξ)=ξm∗zmL_{m}(z;\xi)=\xi^{m}\ast z^{m} is irreducible in 𝒜ℚ​[ξ,z]{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{Q}}[{\xi,z}].

Proof:  By a theorem proved by I. Schur [Sc1], we know that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, the Laguerre polynomials Lm​(z)L_{m}(z) in one variable is irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. Hence, by Eq. (5.9) and Lemma 5.8, the theorem holds.  □\Box

Note that I. Schur also proved in [Sc2] that the generalized Laguerre polynomials Lm[1]​(z)L_{m}^{[1]}(z) (m≥0)(m\geq 0) in one variable are also irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. Furthermore, M. Filaseta and T.-Y. Lam proved in [FL] that, for any non-negative k∈ℚk\in{\mathbb{Q}}, all but finitely many of the generalized Laguerre polynomials Lm[k]​(z)L_{m}^{[k]}(z) (m≥0)(m\geq 0) in one variable are irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. Hence, by a similar argument as for Theorem 5.9, we also have the following theorem.

Theorem 5.10.

Let ξ\xi and zz be two commutative free variables. Then, for any k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, all but only finitely many of the polynomials z−k​(ξm∗zm+k)z^{-k}(\xi^{m}\ast z^{m+k}) and ξ−k​(ξm+k∗zm)\xi^{-k}(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m}) (m∈ℕ)(m\in{\mathbb{N}}) are irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

Next, we re-prove some important properties of the generalized Laguerre polynomials by using their expressions given in Theorem 5.2. For simplicity, we here only consider the one-variable case. Similar results for the multi-variable generalized Laguerre polynomials can be simply derived from the one-variable case via Eq. (5.3).

First, let us look at the following recurrent formulas of the Laguerre polynomials in one variable.

Proposition 5.11.

For any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(5.34) (m+1)​Lm+1​(z)\displaystyle(m+1)L_{m+1}(z) =(2​m+1−z)​Lm​(z)−m​Lm−1​(z),\displaystyle=(2m+1-z)L_{m}(z)-mL_{m-1}(z),
(5.35) z​Lm′​(z)\displaystyle zL^{\prime}_{m}(z) =m⁡(Lm​(z)−Lm−1​(z))\displaystyle=m(L_{m}(z)-L_{m-1}(z))

Proof:  Note first that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, by Eqs. (2.14) and (2.15), we have

ξ∗zm\displaystyle\xi\ast z^{m} =(ξ−∂)zm=ξzm−mzm−1,\displaystyle=(\xi-\partial)z^{m}=\xi z^{m}-mz^{m-1},
z∗ξm\displaystyle z\ast\xi^{m} =(z−δ)​ξm=z​ξm−m​ξm−1.\displaystyle=(z-\delta)\xi^{m}=z\xi^{m}-m\xi^{m-1}.

Hence, we also have

ξ∗z\displaystyle\xi\ast z =ξ​z−1,\displaystyle=\xi z-1,
ξ​zm\displaystyle\xi z^{m} =ξ∗zm+m​zm−1,\displaystyle=\xi\ast z^{m}+mz^{m-1},
z​ξm\displaystyle z\xi^{m} =z∗ξm+m​ξm−1.\displaystyle=z\ast\xi^{m}+m\xi^{m-1}.

By the last three equations above and also Eq. (2.23), we have

(ξ​z−1)​(ξm∗zm)\displaystyle(\xi z-1)(\xi^{m}\ast z^{m}) =(ξ∗z)​(ξm∗zm)=(z​ξm)∗(ξ​zm)\displaystyle=(\xi\ast z)(\xi^{m}\ast z^{m})=(z\xi^{m})\ast(\xi z^{m})
=(z∗ξm+m​ξm−1)∗(ξ∗zm+m​zm−1)\displaystyle=(z\ast\xi^{m}+m\xi^{m-1})\ast(\xi\ast z^{m}+mz^{m-1})
=ξm+1∗zm+1+2​m​ξm∗zm+m2​ξm−1∗zm−1.\displaystyle=\xi^{m+1}\ast z^{m+1}+2m\,\xi^{m}\ast z^{m}+m^{2}\xi^{m-1}\ast z^{m-1}.

Multiply (−1)m/m!(-1)^{m}/m! to the equation above and then apply Eq. (5.9), we get

(ξ​z−1)​Lm​(ξ​z)=−(m+1)​Lm+1​(ξ​z)+2​m​Lm​(ξ​z)−m​Lm−1​(ξ​z).\displaystyle(\xi z-1)L_{m}(\xi z)=-(m+1)L_{m+1}(\xi z)+2mL_{m}(\xi z)-mL_{m-1}(\xi z).

Replace ξ​z\xi z by zz in the equation above, we get

(z−1)​Lm​(z)=−(m+1)​Lm+1​(z)+2​m​Lm​(z)−m​Lm−1​(z),\displaystyle(z-1)L_{m}(z)=-(m+1)L_{m+1}(z)+2mL_{m}(z)-mL_{m-1}(z),

Hence Eq. (5.34) follows.

To show Eq. (5.35), by Eqs. (2.15) and (2.30), we have,

ξm∗zm\displaystyle\xi^{m}\ast z^{m} =z∗(ξm∗zm−1)=(z−δ)​(ξm∗zm−1)\displaystyle=z\ast(\xi^{m}\ast z^{m-1})=(z-\delta)(\xi^{m}\ast z^{m-1})
=z⁡(ξm∗zm−1)−m⁡(ξm−1∗zm−1)\displaystyle=z(\xi^{m}\ast z^{m-1})-m(\xi^{m-1}\ast z^{m-1})
=1m​z​∂(ξm∗zm)−m⁡(ξm−1∗zm−1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}z\partial(\xi^{m}\ast z^{m})-m(\xi^{m-1}\ast z^{m-1}).

Multiply (−1)m/m!(-1)^{m}/m! to the equation above and then apply Eq. (5.9), we get

Lm​(ξ​z)=1m​z​∂(Lm​(ξ​z))+Lm−1​(ξ​z)=1m​ξ​z​Lm′​(ξ​z)+Lm−1​(ξ​z).\displaystyle L_{m}(\xi z)=\frac{1}{m}z\partial(L_{m}(\xi z))+L_{m-1}(\xi z)=\frac{1}{m}\xi zL^{\prime}_{m}(\xi z)+L_{m-1}(\xi z).

Replace ξ​z\xi z by zz in the equation above, we get

Lm​(z)=1m​z​Lm′​(z)+Lm−1​(z).\displaystyle L_{m}(z)=\frac{1}{m}zL^{\prime}_{m}(z)+L_{m-1}(z).

Hence Eq. (5.35) follows.  □\Box

Next, we give a new proof for the following important property of the generalized Laguerre polynomials in one variable.

Theorem 5.12.

For any k,m∈ℕk,m\in{\mathbb{N}}, Lm[k]​(z)L_{m}^{[k]}(z) solves the following so-called associated Laguerre differential equation:

(5.36) z​f′′​(z)+(k+1−z)​f′​(z)+m​f​(z)=0.\displaystyle zf^{\prime\prime}(z)+(k+1-z)f^{\prime}(z)+mf(z)=0.

Proof:  First, by Eq. (5.1), we have L0[k]​(z)=1L_{0}^{[k]}(z)=1. It is easy to see that the theorem holds for this case.

Assume m≥1m\geq 1. Then, by Eq. (2.15), we have

ξ⁡(ξm+k∗zm)\displaystyle\xi(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m}) =ξ⁡(z∗(ξm+k∗zm−1))\displaystyle=\xi(z\ast(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1}))
=ξ⁡(z−δ)​(ξm+k∗zm−1)\displaystyle=\xi(z-\delta)(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1})
=ξ​z​(ξm+k∗zm−1)−ξ​δ​(ξm+k∗zm−1).\displaystyle=\xi z(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1})-\xi\delta(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1}).

Add z​∂(ξm+k∗zm−1)z\partial(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1}) to the equation above and apply Eq. (2.21), we have

ξ⁡(ξm+k∗zm)+z​∂(ξm+k∗zm−1)\displaystyle\xi(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m})+z\partial(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1})
=ξz(ξm+k∗zm−1)−(ξδ−z∂)(ξm+k∗zm−1)\displaystyle=\xi z(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1})-(\xi\delta-z\partial)(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1})
=(ξ​z−k−1)​(ξm+k∗zm−1).\displaystyle=(\xi z-k-1)(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m-1}).

By Eq. (2.29), we may re-write the equation above as

ξ⁡(ξm+k∗zm)+1m​z​∂2(ξm+k∗zm)=1m​(ξ​z−k−1)​∂(ξm+k∗zm).\displaystyle\xi(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m})+\frac{1}{m}z\partial^{2}(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m})=\frac{1}{m}(\xi z-k-1)\partial(\xi^{m+k}\ast z^{m}).

Multiply (−1)m​ξ−k−1(m−1)!\frac{(-1)^{m}\xi^{-k-1}}{(m-1)!} to both sides of the equation above and then apply Eq. (5.7), we have

m​Lm[k]​(ξ​z)+z​ξ−1​∂2(Lm[k]​(ξ​z))=(ξ​z−k−1)​ξ−1​∂(Lm[k]​(ξ​z)).\displaystyle mL_{m}^{[k]}(\xi z)+z\xi^{-1}\partial^{2}(L_{m}^{[k]}(\xi z))=(\xi z-k-1)\xi^{-1}\partial(L_{m}^{[k]}(\xi z)).

By the Chain rule, the equation above is same as

m​Lm[k]​(ξ​z)+z​ξ​(∂2Lm[k])​(ξ​z)=(ξ​z−k−1)​(∂Lm[k])​(ξ​z).\displaystyle mL_{m}^{[k]}(\xi z)+z\xi(\partial^{2}L_{m}^{[k]})(\xi z)=(\xi z-k-1)(\partial L_{m}^{[k]})(\xi z).

Replace ξ​z\xi z by zz, or zz by ξ−1​z\xi^{-1}z in the equation above, we get

m​Lm[k]​(z)+z​∂2Lm[k]​(z)=(z−k−1)​∂Lm[k]​(z).\displaystyle mL_{m}^{[k]}(z)+z\partial^{2}L_{m}^{[k]}(z)=(z-k-1)\partial L_{m}^{[k]}(z).

Hence we have proved the theorem.  □\Box

Finally, let us point out the following conjecture on the generalized Laguerre polynomials, which is a special case of Conjecture 3.53.5 in [Z4] for all the classical orthogonal polynomials.

Conjecture 5.13.

For any 𝐤∈ℕn{\bf k}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, the subspace ℳ{\mathcal{M}} of the polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] spanned by the generalized Laguerre polynomials Lα[𝐤]​(z)L^{[\bf k]}_{\alpha}(z) (0≠α∈ℕn)(0\neq\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

Despite the vast amount of known results on the generalized Laguerre polynomials in the literature, the conjecture above is even still open for the classical Laguerre polynomials, (i.e. the case with 𝐤=0{\bf k}=0) in one variable.
